planting.note: Divide rhizomes in early spring just as shoots emerge and set them horizontally 1-2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; this compact Japanese species is slower to bulk up than P. odoratum types but holds its cream leaf edge reliably in deeper shade.

directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally 1-2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. This selection of the naturally more compact Japanese Solomon's seal stays noticeably shorter and denser than the taller P. odoratum and P. multiflorum cultivars, with narrow arching stems lined by leaves edged in a crisp, even white margin from the moment they unfurl. Small, paired, greenish-white bells dangle beneath the stems in late spring, followed by dark berries in fall. Its smaller stature and tighter clumping habit suit it especially well to shaded rock gardens, path edges, and container culture where a full-size Solomon's seal would sprawl too far. Give it a leaf-litter mulch and consistent moisture through the growing season for the cleanest variegation; all parts are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Flore Pleno Solomon's Seal (Double-Flowered Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in early spring or fall and plant horizontally 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade; this old double-flowered heirloom form is rarer and slower to divide than the plain species, so start with a well-established clump.

directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade. This long-cultivated garden sport of common Solomon's seal carries the same gracefully arching, unbranched stems and neat oval foliage as the species, but each dangling flower along the stem is doubled into a small rounded white rosette rather than a single simple bell, giving the plant a fuller, more textured look in bloom during late spring. It is slower to spread than the plain species and prized among collectors of historic shade perennials for its rarity and old-garden character. Plant it where its subtly doubled flowers can be appreciated up close along a shaded path, and mulch with leaf litter to conserve the steady moisture it needs through the growing season. All parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant bulbs just below the soil surface in moist, deeply humus-rich, well-drained but moisture-retaining, slightly acidic soil in part to full shade; this Yunnan form flowers at a younger age and smaller stature than typical Cardiocrinum giganteum, making it more practical for average-size gardens.

directions: Plant bulbs near the soil surface in deeply humus-rich, moist, well-drained but moisture-retentive, slightly acidic soil in part to full shade. This wild-collected botanical variety from Yunnan, China is a markedly more compact and quicker-flowering form of the giant Himalayan lily, typically reaching bulb maturity and blooming after only 3-4 years of vegetative growth rather than the 5-7 years typical of the larger nominate species. It still produces a bold flowering stem, though usually 4-7 feet rather than the towering 10-12 feet of full-size giganteum, topped by a shorter succession of large, white, maroon-throated, fragrant trumpet flowers in midsummer. As with all Cardiocrinum, the flowering bulb dies after seed set but leaves offset bulblets to carry the colony forward. Its smaller footprint makes it a more garden-practical choice than the true giant species for shaded borders where dramatic scale is wanted without quite so much vertical reach.

planting.note: Plant bulbs just below the soil surface in moist, deeply humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in part to full shade; this Japanese species is noticeably smaller and more shade-tolerant than its Himalayan relative and suits an ordinary shaded border better than the giant species.

directions: Plant bulbs near the soil surface in deeply humus-rich, moist, well-drained woodland soil in part to full shade. Native to the cool mountain forests of Japan, this smaller cousin of the giant Himalayan lily forms a modest rosette of broad, glossy, heart-shaped leaves that carpet the woodland floor for several seasons before a slender flowering stem rises, bearing a shorter cluster of pendant, greenish-white to cream, funnel-shaped flowers in summer. Its scale and shade tolerance are far closer to a typical woodland perennial than to the towering Cardiocrinum giganteum, making it a good choice for a shaded Japanese-style or woodland garden where the drama of a giant lily is not needed. As with other Cardiocrinum, the flowering rosette dies after seed set but leaves offset bulbs to continue the colony; keep soil consistently moist and rich in leaf mold to mimic its forest-floor origin.
